897.title: The Karorsinghia misl
897.hook: a misl of the Doaba lands
897.howItsDone: Sikh histories describe each misl by its leaders and its home country; families in Punjab sometimes still remember which misl their village rode with.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Singhpuria misl, named for Singhpura, Nawab Kapur Singh's own riders; your line was the nawab's band. Today, a band that belonged to a stretch of land.

Wedding drums in one village, and the next village over can hear them. Wheat, sugarcane, mango groves: flat green farmland between the Beas and the Sutlej. Punjabis call it the Doaba. A family there knows the families around it, and whose grandfather dug which well. In the misl years, riders from those villages saddled up together and fought as one band. Their neighbors knew them by their leader's name, and the land knew them as its own.
screen: `WEDDING DRUMS ACROSS THE FIELDS.` → `THE DOABA, BETWEEN THE BEAS AND THE SUTLEJ.` → `A BAND FROM ITS VILLAGES.`

segments.voice: Sikh histories say this misl was named for one of its leaders, Karora Singh. So the name carries a person, but the band belonged to a place. Its riders came largely from the Doaba, and that is where their strength sat. A misl was not an army on a map. It was farmers' sons, cousins and neighbors, men who knew which well was sweet and whose field bordered whose. They rode for a village they could name, and when danger passed, they went home to it. Then a later leader, Baghel Singh. Tradition says he took the band far beyond the Doaba, all the way to Delhi. The story Sikhs tell about him there is not mainly about conquest. Tradition says he sought out the places in the city tied to the Gurus, and saw that they were marked. Gurdwaras stand at such places in Delhi today, and Sikh memory links some of them to his search. A band rooted in one patch of farmland reached a far city, and what it is remembered for there is remembering. And the plainest point: home ground shaped a misl. A band of the Doaba carried its fields, wells and neighbors into its fights and its peace. The faith was the same in every band. Place gave each one its own accent.

898.title: The Shaheedan misl
898.hook: the martyrs' misl, linked to Baba Deep Singh
898.howItsDone: In Ardas, the prayer said at the close of Sikh services, Sikhs remember the martyrs who held to their faith; Baba Deep Singh is remembered at gurdwaras in Amritsar and at Damdama Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Karora Singh, and a band rooted in the Doaba; your line was a band of the doaba. Today, a band named not for a place or a leader.

The misls you've met this block mostly wear a name from a map or a family tree: a village, a leader, a stretch of country. The Nishanwalias took theirs from a duty. Today's band called itself after the dead. Not after a defeat, and not exactly after a grief: after the people who had given their lives, whose example the riders meant to keep. Shaheed is the Punjabi word for a martyr. This is the Shaheedan misl, the band of the martyrs.
screen: `A VILLAGE, A LEADER, A COUNTRY, A DUTY.` → `ONE BAND CHOSE THE DEAD.` → `SHAHEED: A MARTYR.`

segments.voice: Sikh tradition ties this band to Baba Deep Singh. This path has told his story: the old scholar who left his study at Damdama Sahib to defend the Harmandir and who, tradition says, fought on to reach the holy precinct even after a mortal wound. The Shaheedan misl is remembered as the band that grew from those around him, keeping his name and his place alive. A name tells riders who they are before anyone gives an order. A band called after a village rides for that village. A band called after martyrs rides with them, in a sense: every time someone said the name, the dead were in the room. Then the center. Tradition links the band to Damdama Sahib, where Baba Deep Singh had worked with the scripture. A band named for those who died for the faith kept close to the place where the faith was copied, read and taught. Sword and book in the same hands, a pairing Sikh tradition holds dear. The hardest part: a name like this could become a boast. Sikh memory doesn't treat martyrdom as a prize to chase. In Ardas, the daily prayer, Sikhs remember those who gave their heads and did not give up their faith, and they ask for the same steadiness, not for a death. The martyrs are remembered so the living can stand straight.

899.title: The Phulkian states
899.hook: Patiala, Nabha and Jind, often counted apart from the twelve
899.howItsDone: Sikh histories tell the story of Phul and Guru Har Rai's blessing, and gurdwaras in the former Phulkian lands, such as those in Patiala, are part of Sikh life in the Malwa region today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shaheed, the martyr, and a band that kept the martyrs' memory; your line was the martyrs' band. Today, a family of chiefs who stood a little to one side.

A hungry boy is brought before Guru Har Rai. Sikh tradition tells it simply: an uncle brings two small brothers to the Guru, and one of them pats his own empty stomach. The Guru looks at the child and blesses him: his house will grow, and it will feed many. The boy's name was Phul. Generations later, the families who traced their line to him ruled three states south of the Sutlej: Patiala, Nabha and Jind.
screen: `A HUNGRY BOY BEFORE GURU HAR RAI.` → `A BLESSING ON HIS HOUSE.` → `PATIALA, NABHA AND JIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the puzzle. Some lists of the twelve misls include the Phulkian states; others set them apart. Both habits have reasons. One is the river. The Phulkian chiefs held the Malwa country, south of the Sutlej: different neighbors, different dangers, different deals. Another is how they ruled. A misl was a band of equals around a chief, joined to the others in the Dal Khalsa. The Phulkian houses grew more like ruling families, leadership passing down a line, the chief becoming a raja. Patiala's founder, Ala Singh, is remembered for building a state, and for making terms with the powers around him at times when other bands were fighting them. Sikh histories judge those terms in more than one way: some call them shrewd survival, some a step away from the Dal Khalsa. So why are they here at all? Because the story starts with the Guru's blessing. The Phulkian families traced their rise to that hungry boy, and they built and supported gurdwaras across their lands. They stood apart in politics and stayed inside the same faith, the same scripture, the same Guru's house. A family can live in a different town and still sit at the same table on the big days.

900.title: Twice a year at Amritsar
900.hook: the misls met as the Sarbat Khalsa at Vaisakhi and Diwali to decide together before the Granth
900.howItsDone: Sikhs still speak of the Sarbat Khalsa and the gurmata, and Sikh congregations take decisions before the Guru Granth Sahib, often ending with Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Phul, and the Phulkian houses south of the river; your line was apart, yet related. Today, the days when everyone came together.

Who decides, when nobody is king? The misl chiefs argued over villages, grazing and who owed whom; some had fought each other. No ruler stood over them, and each answered to his own riders. Yet at Vaisakhi in spring and Diwali in autumn, Sikh histories say, they came to Amritsar, sat down together, and put the Guru Granth Sahib in front of them.
screen: `NOBODY IS KING.` → `RIVALS, EACH WITH HIS OWN RIDERS.` → `ONE PLACE, TWICE A YEAR.`

segments.voice: The gathering had a name: the Sarbat Khalsa. Sarbat means all, the whole: not one chief's council, not a king's court. In principle, every band had a place in it. Then where they sat. Tradition says the assembly met before the Guru Granth Sahib, near the Akal Takht. The scripture wasn't decoration; it was the presence they decided in front of. A chief who might shout in his own camp had to speak here as one Sikh among others before the Guru. Then what came out of it. A decision reached this way was called a gurmata, which Sikhs describe as a resolution of the Guru, made by the gathered Khalsa in the Guru's presence. Once agreed, it bound the bands together. Sikh histories say this is how the misls chose shared leaders, planned joint campaigns, and set their quarrels aside, at least for a season. And notice the season. Vaisakhi and Diwali were already festival days, when people came to Amritsar anyway to bathe in the pool and see the Harmandir. The meeting rode on the back of the celebration: faith first, then business, and the business done in faith's presence. A people with no single ruler found a single voice, twice a year.

901.title: The bungas
901.hook: the misls built rest-houses round the sacred pool for pilgrims and defenders
901.howItsDone: Pilgrims to the Harmandir Sahib today stay in the guest houses (sarais) of the complex, free of charge, and some old bunga buildings still stand near the pool.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurmata: the whole Khalsa deciding before the Guru; your line was decide before the guru. Today, where all those riders slept.

A blanket unrolled on a brick floor, a few steps from the water. A horse tied up outside. A rider who has come a long way leaves his things in a room with thick walls and goes down to bathe in the pool and bow at the Harmandir. That room isn't an inn. Sikh histories say the misls built such houses around the sacred pool, one by one, each put up by a chief or a band. Today's word is what they were called: bunga.
screen: `A BLANKET ON A BRICK FLOOR.` → `A FEW STEPS FROM THE WATER.` → `HOUSES RISE AROUND THE POOL.`

segments.voice: A bunga did three jobs at once. The first was rest. Pilgrims coming to the Harmandir needed somewhere to stay, and a bunga gave them a place by the pool, close enough to hear the kirtan, the sung scripture, with no inn to find and no room to bargain for. The second was defense. In these years the Harmandir had been attacked and damaged, as this path has told, so a bunga was no light guesthouse. Tradition describes strong buildings, some with high walls, where defenders could stay and keep watch over the pool and the shrine. Rest and guard duty under one roof. The third job was belonging. Each bunga was tied to a misl, a chief or a community, so riders from that band knew where their place was. A misl miles away the rest of the year had a doorway on the edge of the sacred pool. Some histories call the building of the Akal Takht itself the Akal Bunga; it faces the Harmandir across the causeway. The precinct has been rebuilt over the years, and most of the old bungas are gone, though a few still stand. The idea is worth keeping: around the Harmandir, people built rooms for strangers to rest in.

902.title: The Ramgarhia towers
902.hook: two tall towers built to guard the Harmandir still stand
902.howItsDone: Pilgrims at the Harmandir Sahib complex in Amritsar can see the towers of the Ramgarhia Bunga near the edge of the precinct, and Sikh histories remember Jassa Singh Ramgarhia as their builder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bungas: houses round the sacred pool for rest and for watch; your line was rest by the pool. Today, the bunga that grew upward.

Stand on the marble walkway around the pool at the Harmandir, look away from the golden shrine, and two brick towers rise above the rooftops near the edge of the complex. They don't glitter. They look like what they were: lookouts. Sikh tradition says they belong to the bunga of Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, the carpenter's son this block met earlier. Rest-houses once ringed the pool; this one still stands for people to point to.
screen: `TWO BRICK TOWERS ABOVE THE ROOFS.` → `NOT GOLD: LOOKOUTS.` → `JASSA SINGH RAMGARHIA'S BUNGA.`

segments.voice: A wall keeps people out; a tower lets you see them coming. In years when, as this path has told, armies came to Amritsar more than once, the people who loved the Harmandir needed early warning. From a tower, a watchman could see the roads and fields beyond the city long before anyone at the pool. So the towers are about attention. Somebody climbs up, stays up and looks, while others below bathe, pray and sleep. Guarding, in this picture, is mostly patience: hours of nothing, for the one moment that matters. Now notice who built them. Jassa Singh Ramgarhia came, tradition says, from a carpenter's family, a family of builders. His band's gift to the Harmandir was not mainly gold. It was a building, made to protect someone else's prayers. And notice the word still. Much of what stood round the pool in the misl years has been rebuilt or cleared, but these lookouts remain, and pilgrims walk past them to the shrine. They've become a sign: a sacred place is something people have chosen to guard. The Harmandir sits low, at the level of the water, with doors open on every side; in Sikh telling, those doors are a welcome to all. Just beyond that openness, someone built towers so the welcome could keep going.

903.title: When the misls quarreled
903.hook: as danger faded, rivalry grew between the misls
903.howItsDone: Sikh histories tell the misl rivalries frankly, and Sikhs read Guru Arjan's hymn on Ang 1299 of the Guru Granth Sahib about having no enemy and no stranger.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ramgarhia towers, plain brick lookouts guarding the Harmandir; your line was guarding towers. Today, the story turns a little sour.

A family pulls together beautifully at a funeral or in a hospital waiting room. Everyone brings food, nobody keeps score. Then the crisis passes, and months later two siblings aren't speaking over who got the good china. Sikh histories tell a story with the same shape. For a long time the misls were hunted, and they rode together because they had to. Then the hunters grew weaker, the misls held land, and the old enemy was no longer at the gate.
screen: `TOGETHER IN THE CRISIS.` → `APART WHEN IT PASSES.` → `THE MISLS HOLD THE LAND.`

segments.voice: While the danger was great, Sikh histories say, the bands needed one another. They met as the Sarbat Khalsa, agreed a gurmata, and rode under shared leaders. But once the misls held territory, each chief had something to lose, and something to gain at a neighbor's expense: border villages, river crossings, revenue, marriages that tied one house to another, or failed to. The quarrels were not about faith. The chiefs bowed at the same Harmandir and heard the same scripture. They were about land, pride and who would lead. One story shows it. Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, the builder of yesterday's towers, was, Sikh histories say, pushed out of his lands for a time by rival chiefs who had once ridden beside him, and he lived beyond the Sutlej until he could come back. Other misls fought, made peace and fought again, and the gatherings at Amritsar grew harder to hold together. Set that beside their scripture. In a hymn of Guru Arjan in the Guru Granth Sahib, on Ang 1299, the singer says, in paraphrase, that no one is his enemy and no one a stranger; he has come to get along with everyone. Hearing it didn't stop the quarrels. That's the honest part of this story: unity under pressure is real, but it's easier than unity at ease.
screen: `THE DANGER LIFTED.` · `LAND, PRIDE AND WHO WOULD LEAD.` · `RAMGARHIA PUSHED ACROSS THE SUTLEJ.` · `NO ONE IS MY ENEMY.` · then, large: `DANGER GONE, RIVALRY GREW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've drifted into competing with or quietly resenting, a sibling, a coworker, an old friend, and remember a time you were on the same side. Ask what the rivalry is really about, maybe something small, land, pride, who leads, and think of one move that would cool it; Waheguru on each breath out, if you pray.

Sarbat Khalsa, the gathering that once bound the misls. Once danger faded, they quarreled over land and leadership, even sharing one scripture.
